question: When can deliberately discarding label-relevant features lower prediction risk in high-dimensional ridge regression, and is that effect distinct from interpolation-driven double descent?

key_findings.claim: The analysis cleanly separates estimation bias, estimator variance, and the irreducible misspecification cost introduced by feature removal.
key_findings.evidence: A Gaussian feature-response model is passed through a noisy projection before fitting ridge regression. Equations 10-15 decompose risk relative to the original conditional mean into regression bias, training-sample variance, and misspecification bias equal to the lost signal, sigma-squared times (1-eta) times SNR.

key_findings.claim: Removing weak-signal coordinates can improve generalization because its variance reduction can dominate its small misspecification penalty.
key_findings.evidence: In the proportional P,N limit with isotropic features and a diagonal noiseless projection, the high-pass path reduces the retained feature fraction q faster than retained signal eta. Its risk has an interior minimum for both under- and over-parameterized examples, whereas removing high-signal coordinates first produces harmful behavior.

key_findings.claim: The paper successfully distinguishes its interior optimum from the interpolation peak within its solvable model.
key_findings.evidence: For fixed small ridge, all paths that cross effective ratio q gamma = 1 exhibit the interpolation ridge. Equations 29-30 then optimize ridge strength separately at each q and eta, removing that ridge; Figure 4 still shows nonmonotone high-pass risk while low- and random-pass risk become monotone.

key_findings.claim: The coarse-graining oracle already knows feature relevance, so the theory explains a benefit conditional on successful supervised selection rather than how to discover the removable features.
key_findings.evidence: The high-pass construction orders coordinates by their contribution to the true coefficient-weighted signal, while the manuscript explicitly notes that physically achievable paths depend on the unknown signal distribution. No estimator of eta, selection-error analysis, or cost for learning the projection from finite data is included.

anchors.section: Definition of three coarse-graining paths and footnote 28

key_findings.claim: The data-augmentation interpretation is a motivating analogy, not a result established by the experiments.
key_findings.evidence: All calculations and simulations use linear Gaussian data, isotropic covariance, coordinate projections, and squared loss. The discussion maps augmentation to invariance against low-relevance details, but evaluates no image augmentation, nonlinear model, learned representation, or distribution shift.

method.core_idea: Treat data coarse graining as a projection that trades lost predictive signal for a smaller effective feature dimension, and solve the resulting ridge-regression risk in the proportional high-dimensional limit.
method.mechanism: Random-matrix asymptotics express prediction risk as a function of sample ratio gamma, retained feature fraction q, retained signal eta, SNR, and ridge lambda; high-, low-, and random-pass projection paths traverse this risk surface differently.
assumptions: Features are Gaussian and, for the closed-form examples, isotropic.
The response is linear with homoscedastic Gaussian noise.
P and N grow together at fixed P/N.
The projection is diagonal and noiseless in the analyzed examples, and its ordering can use true feature relevance.
Train and test inputs pass through the same fixed channel.

techniques.role: Removes coordinates in an order determined by their true contribution to the response signal.
Produces deterministic bias and variance expressions as feature and sample counts grow proportionally.
Retunes regularization at each projection level to separate coarse-graining nonmonotonicity from double descent.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic isotropic Gaussian linear regression across under- and over-parameterized sample ratios
evaluations.metric: Asymptotic prediction risk versus fraction of response information removed
evaluations.result: High-pass removal has an interior risk minimum; low-pass removal is detrimental; paths crossing q gamma = 1 show an interpolation peak at small ridge
evaluations.baseline: No coarse graining plus random-pass and high-signal-first projections

evaluations.setting: Same solvable model with analytically optimal ridge at each coarse-graining level
evaluations.result: The interpolation ridge disappears while the high-pass interior optimum remains
evaluations.baseline: Low-pass and random-pass paths become monotone under optimal regularization

limitations: Author-stated: the closed-form study uses isotropic linear-Gaussian data and does not cover kernels, neural networks, anisotropic covariance, or realistic learned coarse graining.
Reviewer-identified: relevance-aware selection uses population signal unavailable to a learner and ignores projection-estimation error.
Reviewer-identified: simulations verify the asymptotic formulas but provide no real-data evidence for the augmentation claim.
failure_modes: Selection noise can remove genuinely predictive coordinates and reverse the variance benefit.
Correlated features can make coordinate-level signal rankings unstable or redundant.
A train-time-only or distribution-dependent transform can create train-test mismatch.
For abundant data, variance is already small and lost signal can dominate any dimensionality benefit.
reusable_insights: Evaluate feature removal on a two-dimensional frontier of retained signal and effective dimension rather than dimension alone.
Retuning regularization is a strong control when claiming that pruning or projection has an effect beyond double descent.
A useful coarse-graining method needs an error-aware relevance estimator, not merely an oracle ordering.
open_questions: How much relevance-estimation error can the interior risk optimum tolerate at finite sample size?
Does an analogous retained-signal versus effective-dimension law predict augmentation gains for nonlinear representation learners?
Can coarse-graining paths be learned using only training data without leaking target information into model selection?

competitive_landscape.title: Information bottleneck theory of high-dimensional regression: relevancy, efficiency and optimality
competitive_landscape.difference: Studies relevant and residual information encoded by regression algorithms; the reviewed paper moves the intervention upstream to an explicit feature channel and characterizes prediction risk along signal-removal paths.

competitive_landscape.title: No Double Descent in Principal Component Regression: A High-Dimensional Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Analyzes unsupervised top-eigenspace projection under a spiked covariance model and distribution shift; the reviewed method orders isotropic coordinates by supervised response relevance and isolates an interior signal-variance tradeoff.

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel regression in high dimensions: Refined analysis beyond double descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows that kernel-regression risk can be monotone, bell-shaped, or double-descent-like depending on spectrum and regularization; it does not intervene by discarding features according to response relevance.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalisation error in learning with random features and the hidden manifold model
competitive_landscape.difference: Derives risk for random and orthogonal nonlinear features with correlated latent data, covering richer representations but not the reviewed paper's supervised coarse-graining continuum.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims an analytical explanation for why lossy, relevance-aware coarse graining can improve prediction and shows the effect persists after optimal regularization removes double descent.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Equations 15 and 20-30 derive the bias-variance-misspecification tradeoff, and Figures 2-4 compare coarse-graining paths with fixed and optimal ridge.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clean separation of response-signal retention from effective dimension, plus the optimal-ridge control, is a useful theoretical contribution. Its practical novelty is narrower: the beneficial path assumes oracle relevance and the paper does not yet demonstrate a learnable augmentation or pruning algorithm.

reviewer_notes: Read all seven extracted pages, including derivation, figures, discussion, limitations, and references. Competitor records were checked against primary arXiv/PMLR pages on 2026-08-23. Claims about oracle access and the scope of the augmentation analogy are reviewer inferences.
